en: Thus have I heard: Majjhima Nikāya 75, the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus at a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma, on a grass mat in the fire-hall of a brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Kammāsadhamma for alms.
Having walked for alms in Kammāsadhamma, after his meal, returning from his almsround, he approached a certain grove for the day’s abiding.
Having entered that grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan.
There, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya saw a grass mat spread out in the brahmin’s fire-hall.
Having seen him, he said this to the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan:
"Whose is this grass mat spread out in your fire-chamber, Master Bhāradvāja? It seems to me it is suitable for the bed of an ascetic.
"There is, Master Māgaṇḍiya, an ascetic Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan."
Furthermore, this excellent report of the venerable Gotama has spread abroad:

"Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with clear vision and virtuous conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
For that Blessed Gotama, this bed has been prepared."
“Alas, Master Bhāradvāja, we have seen what is ill-seen!
Alas, Master Bhāradvāja, we have seen what is ill-seen!
For we have seen the bed of that Blessed Gotama, the destroyer of beings.”
“Guard this speech, Māgandiya; guard this speech, Māgandiya.
For many wise khattiyas, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise ascetics have placed their confidence in that Blessed Gotama; they are disciplined in the noble method and skilled in the Dhamma.”
“Even if we were to see that venerable Gotama face-to-face, Master Bhāradvāja, we would say to his face:
‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer.
And why is that? Because—”
"In this way, you descend upon our Sutta.
"If it does not trouble the venerable Māgandiya, I shall report it to the ascetic Gotama.
"Let the venerable Bhāradvāja be at ease; let him say exactly what was said."
With his purified divine ear-element, which surpasses that of humans, the Blessed One heard this conversation between the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan’s fire-chamber; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared grass mat.
Then the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Bhāradvāja, did you have any conversation with the wanderer Māgandiya concerning this very grass mat?"
When this was said, the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, moved and with his hair standing on end, said this to the Blessed One:
“This very thing, indeed, we wished to report to Master Gotama;
yet Master Gotama has explained it even though it had not been told.”
For this conversation between the Blessed One and the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan had been left unfinished.
Then, while walking and wandering for exercise, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya approached the sacrificial fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan where the Blessed One was staying;
having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. As the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"The eye, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in forms, rejoices in forms, and finds delight in forms.
That [eye] has been subdued, guarded, protected, and restrained by the Tathāgata, and he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint."
“Was it with reference to this, Māgaṇḍiya, that you said:
‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of beings’?
“Indeed, Master Gotama, it was precisely with reference to this that I spoke.”
“The ascetic Gotama is a nihilist.
For what reason?
Because it is thus that he descends into our discourses.
“The ear, Māgandiya, delights in sounds … the nose, Māgandiya, delights in odors … the tongue,
Māgandiya, delights in tastes, takes pleasure in tastes, and rejoices in tastes.”
“The Tathāgata’s teeth are guarded, protected, restrained, and well-disciplined; he teaches the Dhamma for their restraint.
Was it with reference to this, Māgaṇḍiya, that you said:
‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of beings’?”
“Indeed, Master Gotama, it was with reference to this very point that I said:
‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of beings.
For what reason? Because he does not allow his disciples to eat meat.”
“For in this way our discourse is consistent with the Sutta.
“The body, Māgandiya, delights in tactile objects and rejoices in tactile objects...
[and so on] ...the mind, Māgandiya, delights in mental phenomena, rejoices in mental phenomena, and finds joy in mental phenomena.”
Thus the Tathāgata is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained, and he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of such restraint.
Was it with reference to this, Māgaṇḍiya, that you said:
“The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of beings”?
“Indeed, Master Gotama, it was with reference to this very point that I said:
‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of beings.
For what reason? Because he does not allow his disciples to eat meat.”
"For in this way it accords with our Sutta.
"What do you think, Māgandiya:
Suppose here someone had previously enjoyed forms cognizable by the eye that were desirable, lovely, and pleasing..."
Regarding those forms that are dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of passion: at a later time,
having understood as they really are the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding forms themselves,
he would abandon craving for forms, dispel the fever for forms, and dwell with thirst departed and his mind inwardly calmed.
"But what, Māgandiya, would you say to him?
"Nothing at all, Master Gotama.
"What do you think, Māgandiya: [text continues]"
‘Here, someone [is affected] by sounds cognizable by the ear … by odors cognizable by the nose … by flavors cognizable by the tongue …’ [and so on].

He may have formerly enjoyed tactile objects cognizable by the body— objects that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust. At a later time,
having understood as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger,
and the escape regarding those very tactile objects, he abandons craving for tactile objects and dispels the fever for tactile objects.
“Free from thirst, with a mind calmed within, he would dwell.
But what, Māgandiya, would you say to him?
“Nothing at all, Master Gotama.”
“Moreover, Māgaṇḍiya, formerly when I was a householder, I lived endowed with and provided with the five cords of sensual pleasure:
with forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
with sounds cognizable by the ear... [and so on]...”
With odors cognizable by the nose that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust; with flavors cognizable by the tongue...
with tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.
Māgandiya, I had three palaces:
one for the rainy season, one for the winter, and one for the summer.
During the four months of the rainy season, Māgandiya, while being entertained by female musicians in the rainy-season palace, I did not descend from the upper story of that palace.
Thus, at a later time, having understood as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding sensual pleasures,
I abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, dispelled the fever of sensual pleasures, and dwelt with thirst departed and my mind inwardly stilled.

Thus, I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, and indulging in sensual pleasures.
I have no longing for them, nor do I find delight therein. And why is that?
Māgaṇḍiya, as for that delight which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states—
even if it remains having attained celestial bliss—
I do not envy one who delights in such delight; I do not find pleasure therein.

"Just as, Māgaṇḍiya, a householder or a householder’s son—wealthy, with great riches and vast possessions—might enjoy himself, provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye...
[and so on] ...tangibles that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust."

Thus, having practiced good conduct by body, having practiced good conduct by speech, and having practiced good conduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he might be reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
There, surrounded by a host of nymphs in the Nandana Grove, endowed and possessed of the fivefold divine sense-pleasures, he would enjoy himself.
He might then see a householder or a householder’s son who was likewise endowed and possessed of the fivefold sense-pleasures and enjoying himself.
"What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Would that son of the gods— surrounded by a host of nymphs in the Nandana grove,
endowed with and possessed of the fivefold divine strands of sensual pleasure,
and enjoying them— envy that householder or householder’s son, or the fivefold human strands of sensual pleasure, or the human [rewards]?"
“Would he be turned back by sensual pleasures?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.
And why is that? Because...”
“Sir Gotama, divine sensual pleasures are more excellent and more sublime than human sensual pleasures.
“In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, formerly when I was a householder, I lived endowed with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure—
forms cognizable by the eye that were desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear, and charming;”
With sounds cognizable by the ear that are connected with sensual desire and provocative of passion...
[and so on] ...with odors cognizable by the nose...
with flavors cognizable by the tongue...
By means of tactile objects cognizable by the body— desirable, agreeable, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust— at a later time,
having understood as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these very sensual pleasures,
he abandons craving for sensual pleasures, dispels the fever of sensual pleasures, and, being free from thirst, within himself...
I dwell with a mind that is completely tranquil.

Yet I see other beings who are not free from passion for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, and indulging in sensual pleasures; I do not envy them, nor do I delight therein. Why is that?
Māgaṇḍiya, as for that delight which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states—
even if it remains having attained celestial bliss—
I do not envy one who delights in such delight; I do not find pleasure therein.

"Just as if, Māgaṇḍiya, a man afflicted with leprosy—his limbs diseased, his body festering, being devoured by worms, and scratching the openings of his wounds with his fingernails—were to heat his body over a pit of glowing embers.
His friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives would bring a physician, a surgeon, for him.
That physician, the surgeon, would then apply medicine to him."
Thus, by means of that medicine, he would be freed from his leprosy; he would be healthy, happy, independent, self-mastering, and able to go wherever he wished.

Suppose he were to see another man who was leprous—his body diseased, his limbs festering, being devoured by worms, scratching at the openings of his wounds with his fingernails, and scorching his body in a pit of glowing embers.
What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya?
“Would that man envy that leper for either his charcoal pit or his taking of medicine?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama. And why is that?”
“For when there is illness, sir Gotama, medicine must be administered; when there is no illness, medicine is not required.

“In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, formerly when I was a householder, I lived provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure—forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, and connected with sensual passion.”
By means of sounds cognizable by the ear that are connected with sensual desire and provocative of passion; ... [and so on] ...
by means of odors cognizable by the nose; ...
by means of flavors cognizable by the tongue; ...
[He is affected] by bodily tangibles that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire,
and provocative of lust. At a later time, having understood as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding sensual pleasures themselves,
he abandons craving for sensual pleasures, dispels the fever of sensual pleasures, and, being free from thirst, [abides] within himself.
I dwell with a mind that is utterly tranquil.

Yet I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, scorched by the fever of sensual pleasures, and indulging in sensual pleasures.
I have no longing for them, nor do I take delight therein.
And why is that? Because,
Māgandiya, whatever delight there is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states—
even if it stands having attained celestial happiness— [that is what I refer to].
Delighting in that pleasure, I have no longing for what is inferior; I do not find delight therein.

Māgaṇḍiya, it is just as if there were a man afflicted with leprosy, his limbs diseased and his body festering, being devoured by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails, and burning his body over a pit of glowing coals.
His friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relations would provide him with a physician and a surgeon.
A physician, a surgeon, might prepare medicine for him.
By means of that medicine, he would be freed from his leprosy; he would become healthy, happy, independent, self-governing, and able to go wherever he wishes.
Then two strong men, seizing him by both arms, would drag him toward a pit of glowing embers.
“What do you think, Māgandiya,
would that man bend his body down just by thinking it?
“Yes, Master Gotama.”
"And for what reason?
Because that fire, Master Gotama, is painful to touch, intensely hot, and fiercely burning.
"What do you think, Māgandiya?"
“Is it only now that this fire is painful to touch, intensely hot, and fiercely burning, or was this fire already painful to touch, intensely hot, and fiercely burning even before?
“It is both now, Master Gotama, and it was also before; this fire is painful to touch, intensely hot, and fiercely burning.
Furthermore, Master Gotama, that leper, with his limbs diseased and his skin festering, being devoured by maggots, [scratches] the openings of his wounds with his fingernails...”
“Distraught and with his faculties impaired, he conceived a perverted perception, thinking that pleasure lay in the very fire that was painful to the touch.
“In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, sensual pleasures have been painful to the touch, greatly burning, and greatly feverish throughout the past;
and sensual pleasures will be painful to the touch, greatly burning, and greatly feverish throughout the future.”
And they are a great fever; even now, in the present time, sensual pleasures are painful to touch, greatly distressing, and a great fever.

Yet these beings, Māgaṇḍiya, who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures and burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, have their faculties impaired and have fallen into the perverted perception that there is happiness in sensual pleasures which are nothing but painful to touch.

"Just as, Māgaṇḍiya, a man suffering from leprosy— with diseased limbs and festering limbs, being devoured by worms and scratching the openings of his wounds with his fingernails— might scorch his body over a pit of glowing embers;
and however much that leprous man, with his diseased and festering limbs,
being devoured by worms and scratching the openings of his wounds with his fingernails, scorches his body over the pit of glowing embers, even so..."

Those openings of wounds are indeed more impure, more foul-smelling, and more putrid, yet there is still some slight pleasure, some slight gratification— namely, that which arises from scratching the openings of those wounds.

In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures and scorched by the fever of sensual pleasures, indulge in sensual pleasures.
In whatever way, Māgaṇḍiya, beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures and scorched by the fever of sensual pleasures,
indulge in those sensual pleasures— in that very same way, the craving for sensual pleasures of those beings increases further,
and they are scorched by the fever of sensual pleasures; yet there arises a mere satisfaction, a mere gratification— namely this:
Dependent upon the five cords of sensual pleasure.
What do you think, Māgandiya,
have you ever seen or heard of a king or a royal minister endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure?
“Having come together and enjoying himself, without having abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, without having dispelled the fever of sensual passion,
could he dwell— having become free from thirst, with a mind calmed within— or has dwelt, or will dwell?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
“Excellent, Māgaṇḍiya! Indeed, Māgaṇḍiya,
I too have neither seen nor heard of a king or a royal minister,

though provided with and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure and indulging in them, who— without abandoning craving for sensual pleasures— [could abandon the fever of sensual pleasures].”
Without having dispelled it, one has lived, lives, or will live free from thirst,
with a mind internally stilled. Furthermore, Māgaṇḍiya, whatever ascetics or brahmins have lived, live, or will live free from thirst, with a mind internally stilled,
all of them [do so] by means of the very arising and passing away of sensual pleasures.

“Having understood, as they truly are, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding sensual pleasures, and having abandoned craving for sensual pleasures and dispelled the fever of sensual passion,
they have lived, do live, or will live with thirst departed and their minds inwardly stilled.
Then, on that occasion, the Blessed One uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Health is the supreme gain,
Nibbāna is the supreme happiness,
and the Eightfold Path is the supreme among paths.”
“...the secure path leading to the Deathless.
When this was said, the wanderer Māgandiya said to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!”
"Truly well-spoken is this by Master Gotama:
‘Health is the supreme gain; Nibbāna is the supreme happiness.
For I too have heard this, Master Gotama, from the ancient wanderers, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking:"
“Health is the highest gain, Nibbāna is the supreme bliss.

“This, Master Gotama, accords with what I have heard from the ancient wanderers, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking. “But as for what you have heard, Māgandiya, from the ancient wanderers, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking:”
“‘Health is the highest gain, Nibbāna is the supreme happiness’—what is that health, and what is that Nibbāna?
When this was said, the wanderer Māgandiya rubbed his own limbs with his hand and said:
“This, Master Gotama, is health; this is Nibbāna.”
“For I, Master Gotama, am currently healthy and happy; nothing afflicts me.
“Māgaṇḍiya, it is just as if there were a man blind from birth, who could not see black or white forms, nor see blue forms, nor see yellow forms...”
He would not see forms that are red, he would not see forms that are madder-red,
he would not see what is level or uneven, he would not see the forms of stars, nor would he see the moon and sun.
Yet he would hear one with sight speaking:
‘Ah, how cleverly dyed indeed is this white cloth! It is beautiful, spotless, and pure.
He would go about searching for such a white cloth.
Then a certain man might deceive him with a soiled, oil-stained hemp rag, saying:
“‘Friend, here for you is this white cloth—handsome, stainless, and pure.
He would accept it, and having accepted it, he would put it on; having put it on, being delighted, he would utter words of delight:
‘Ah, what a skillful white cloth! It is handsome, stainless, and pure!’”
"What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya?

Would that man born blind, knowing and seeing it, take up that saffron-colored rag from the oil-smeared heap, and having taken it up, put it on, and having put it on, utter words of satisfaction, saying:
‘Ah, what a clever, bright, beautiful, spotless, and clean cloth this is!’—or would he do so out of faith in one who has eyes?"

“Because, Master Gotama, not knowing and not seeing, that blind man would take up that saffron-colored cloth smeared with oil, and having taken it up, he would put it on; and having put it on, he would utter words of satisfaction, saying:
‘How cleverly indeed, sir, this white cloth is beautiful, spotless, and pure!’—all through faith in one who has eyes.
“In exactly the same way, Māgandiya, the wanderers of other sects are blind and sightless; they do not know health and do not see Nibbāna, yet they recite this verse:”
“Health is the supreme gain; Nibbāna is the supreme bliss.
Māgaṇḍiya, this verse was spoken by the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past:
“Health is the supreme gain...”
“Nirvana is the supreme bliss;
and the Eightfold Path is the safest way leading to the Deathless.”
This, in turn, has gradually become a verse for worldlings.

But this body, Māgandiya, is a mass of disease, a mass of abscesses, a mass of arrows, a mass of misfortune, a mass of afflictions; yet you say of this body—a mass of disease, a mass of abscesses, a mass of arrows, a mass of misfortune, a mass of afflictions:
“This, Master Gotama, is health; this is Nibbāna.”
“Because you do not possess that noble eye, Māgandiya, by which noble eye you might know health and see Nibbāna.
“I have such confidence in Master Gotama.
Master Gotama is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might know health and see Nibbāna.”
“Māgaṇḍiya, it is just as if there were a man born blind;
he would not see forms that are black or white, he would not see forms that are blue, he would not see forms that are yellow,
he would not see forms that are red, and he would not see forms that are crimson.”
He would not see even or uneven things, nor would he see the forms of the stars, nor would he see the moon and the sun.
His friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relatives would attend upon him with a physician and a surgeon.
That physician and surgeon would then prepare medicine for him.
“Thus, by resorting to that medicine, he would not produce eyes, nor would he purify his eyes.
What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya?
Would that physician not merely partake in weariness and frustration?”
“Yes, Master Gotama.
“In the same way, Māgandiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma thus:
‘This is health; this is Nibbāna,’ you would not understand that health, nor would you see that Nibbāna.”
“Then there would be weariness for me, there would be vexation for me.
“I have such confidence in Master Gotama that Master Gotama is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might know health and see Nibbāna.”
“Māgaṇḍiya, it is just as if there were a man born blind;
he would not see forms that are black or white, he would not see forms that are blue, he would not see forms that are yellow,
he would not see forms that are red, and he would not see forms that are crimson.”
He would not see the stars, whether even or unevenly positioned, nor would he see the moon and the sun.
Yet he might hear someone with sight saying:
"Oh, what a clever, white cloth! How beautiful, spotless, and pure it is!"
Thus he would go about searching for a white cloth.
Then a certain man might deceive him with a soiled oil-stained hemp rag, saying:
"O man, here is a white cloth for you—handsome, stainless, and clean."
He would accept it, and having accepted it, he would apply it.
His friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relatives would bring a physician and surgeon to attend him.
That physician and surgeon would prepare medicine for him.
There is an upward purgative, a downward purgative, collyrium, counter-collyrium, and nasal medication.
By means of that medicine, he might restore his sight or clear his vision.
With the restoration of his sight, whatever desire and lust he had for that safflower-dyed cloth smeared with oil would be abandoned.
He would burn that man even more than an enemy and burn him even more than an adversary; indeed, he would think him worthy of being deprived of life, thinking:
“Alas, sir, for a long time I have been deceived, cheated, and deluded by this man with his oil-stained, coarse hemp cloth!
‘O man, here is a white garment, beautiful, stainless, and pure! (so he would think).
In the same way, Māgandiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma thus:
“This is health; this is Nibbāna,” you would know health and you would see Nibbāna.
With the arising of that vision, whatever desire and lust you had for the five aggregates of clinging would be abandoned;
yet, you might think:
"Alas, for a long time indeed I have been deceived, cheated, and deluded by this mind!"

"For I, grasping at form itself, have grasped; grasping at feeling itself, I have grasped; grasping at perception itself, I have grasped; grasping at volitional formations themselves, I have grasped; grasping at consciousness itself, I have grasped.
With grasping as condition, becoming comes to be; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering."
“I have such confidence in Master Gotama that Master Gotama is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might rise from this seat no longer blind.
“In that case, Māgandiya, you should associate with true persons.”
Since you, Māgandiya, will associate with true persons, you will hear the true Dhamma;
since you, Māgandiya, will hear the true Dhamma, you will practice in accordance with the Dhamma;
since you, Māgandiya, will practice in accordance with the Dhamma, you will know for yourself and see for yourself.
These are diseases, abscesses, and arrows;
here these diseases, abscesses, and arrows cease without remainder.

For me, with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
"Thus occurs the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
When this was said, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya said to the Blessed One:
"Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!"
"Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost,
or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with sight might see forms— in the same way,
the Dhamma has been made clear by Master Gotama in many ways."

“I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going-forth in the presence of Master Gotama; may I receive the full ordination. “Māgaṇḍiya, whoever has previously belonged to another sect and desires the going-forth in this Dhamma and Discipline must first undergo a four-month probationary period. After the lapse of those four months, if it is approved by the bhikkhus and deemed fit, he may receive the going-forth and the full ordination to become a bhikkhu.

However, there is an exception for one who was formerly a member of a sect of naked ascetics. “Master Gotama, I am satisfied with this probationary period. I shall undergo it. Then Māgaṇḍiya the naked ascetic underwent the four-month probationary period. After the lapse of those four months, being approved by the bhikkhus and deemed fit, he received the going-forth and the full ordination to become a bhikkhu. Not long after his full ordination, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Māgaṇḍiya, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Māgaṇḍiya became one of the arahants. Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, the Venerable Māgaṇḍiya has declared final knowledge thus: ‘I understand: Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. “Bhikkhus, Māgaṇḍiya is not one who speaks after having fully understood. Māgaṇḍiya is one who speaks after having fully understood. “But, venerable sir, how did the Venerable Māgaṇḍiya declare final knowledge? “Bhikkhus, when Māgaṇḍiya was still a follower of another sect, he came to me and said: ‘I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going-forth in the presence of Master Gotama; may I receive the full ordination. ‘Māgaṇḍiya, whoever has previously belonged to another sect and desires the going-forth in this Dhamma and Discipline must first undergo a four-month probationary period... ‘Master Gotama, I am satisfied with this probationary period. I shall undergo it. Then Māgaṇḍiya the naked ascetic underwent the four-month probationary period. After the lapse of those four months, being approved by the bhikkhus and deemed fit, he received the going-forth and the full ordination to become a bhikkhu. Not long after his full ordination, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Māgaṇḍiya, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Māgaṇḍiya became one of the arahants. It was in this way, bhikkhus, that the Venerable Māgaṇḍiya declared final knowledge.”

“Having received the full ordination, he remains on probation for four months; at the end of those four months, the bhikkhus, with minds inclined toward him, grant him the going-forth and ordain him into the state of a bhikkhu.
Moreover, I recognize a distinction between individuals in this matter.”

“Venerable sir, if those who were formerly members of other sects, desiring the going-forth and desiring the full ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline, must wait four months as probationers, and at the end of those four months, if the bhikkhus are satisfied with them, they grant them the going-forth and the full ordination into the state of a bhikkhu;
then I shall wait four years as a probationer. [At the end of the four years...]
"At the end of the rains retreat, let the monks, with hearts inclined toward it, grant him the going-forth and ordain him into the state of a monk.
Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received ordination.
Not long after his ordination, the Venerable Māgaṇḍiya, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute...

Dwelling thus, before long he—having realized for himself through direct knowledge and having attained it in this very life—that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness—remained there.
He directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
And so the venerable Māgaṇḍiya became one of the arahants.
The Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, the fifth, is finished.
